newsitem.title: USA: GM strike deadline extended, others draw closer.
newsitem.headline: GM strike deadline extended, others draw closer.

text.p: General Motors Corp. worked feverishly to try to avert strikes at three parts plants Friday as one strike deadline was extended indefinitely and two others drew closer.

A walkout at any of the plants could significantly disrupt GM's North American car and truck assembly operations, but a strike at GM's catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wis., would likely cause the broadest and quickest damage.

Bargainers continued talks at the suburban Milwaukee factory late Friday, well past a deadline of 11:59 p.m. EDT on Thursday. Negotiations also continued at a foundry in Saginaw, Mich., and a metal stamping plant in Grand Rapids, Mich., both of which the United Auto Workers union has threatened to strike just before midnight Friday unless deals are reached.

GM and UAW officials said they were encouraged by the deadline extension at the Oak Creek plant, which makes exhaust system catalytic converters for nearly all of GM's North American cars and trucks, as well as customers in Europe and Asia.
A work stoppage at the 870-employee factory would begin to halt production at most of GM's 29 North American car and truck assembly plants within days, GM officials said.

"Last night, we received a proposal late from management, and we are going over that proposal right now to see if it would be acceptable," said Skip Dziedzic, president of UAW Local 1866 in Oak Creek.

In another encouraging sign, talks aimed at ending a strike at GM's Pontiac, Mich., truck plant continued Friday after the first all-night bargaining session since the walkout began more than seven weeks ago.

Until this week, talks have moved slowly at the plant, one of three that make GM's popular full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks. Some analysts view the Oak Creek strike threat and the Friday night strike deadlines in Michigan as moves by the UAW to pressure GM into settling the Pontiac walkout.
About 5,800 workers walked off their jobs at Pontiac on April 22 to underscore their demands for more jobs to ease an increasing workload. UAW Local 594 initially sought 600 new jobs.
GM has resisted, in part because a new-generation pickup truck due next year is expected to require about 30 percent fewer workers to build it.
"Our feelings are that General Motors must realise we're determined to end the unjust treatment of our people," said Jim Abare, an officer of Local 594. "We're not going to back down."

GM's Saginaw foundry employs about 900 workers and makes pistons, rods and transmission parts for various GM vehicles. The Grand Rapids plant, which employes 2,346 hourly workers, stamps out doors, fenders, hoods and other sheet metal parts for various cars and trucks, including GM's all-new minivans.

At Oak Creek, Local 1866 is demanding new restrictions on GM's ability to shift work to outside suppliers and a commitment that GM will continue investing in the catalytic converter business. Future air pollution restrictions are expected to require a new generation of more complex precious-metal catalysts.
GM's stock rose 37.5 cents to $57.25 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
